summary:
Cabo Verde does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Article 71 of the 1886 Penal Code had prohibited unnatural acts. A 2004 amendment removed all provisions on consensual homosexual sex.

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. Civil law blocked a change to a female legal name sought by Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed transgender woman in Cabo Verde who came out in 1997 at age 19 and in a local newspaper in 1998. The inventory holds no later statute or administrative procedure permitting a legal gender change. A visitor whose passport marker differs from presentation should expect no local precedent for documentary flexibility.

Workplace protection does not cover gender identity. Articles 45(2) and 406(3) of the Labour Code have prohibited employment discrimination based on sexual orientation since 2008. A transgender worker therefore has no explicit statutory basis for a workplace complaint on gender identity grounds.

Cabo Verde does not recognise same-sex unions. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva said on 11 July 2017 that same-sex marriage was not on the government agenda. He distanced himself from opposition expressed by MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro after community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Societal discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity was found to continue as a problem in the 2010 United States Department of State human rights report, despite legal provisions protecting homosexual conduct. In a 22 June 2016 interview, Andrade reported verbal violence and two physical attacks, while describing Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people in comparison with other countries on the continent.

Official signals are protective at international level and engaged domestically. Cabo Verde signed United Nations documents in 2008 stating human rights are not limited by sexual orientation or gender identity and in 2011 condemning violence and discrimination against LGBT people. It is one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group, made anti-discrimination commitments in the 2024 Universal Periodic Review, and in 2025 signed a Spain-proposed joint declaration for LGBTQ rights as the only African signatory. LGBTIQ organisations register freely. The state gender-equality institute ICIEG engaged with Pride organising alongside UN Women, which indicates institutional contact points a visitor could approach.
tangentialFactors:
General tolerance findings are relatively high by continental comparison but do not measure attitudes to transgender people specifically. Polls in 2019 to 2021 found 82 percent would accept a homosexual neighbour. A 2020 Afrobarometer poll found 80 percent would welcome or would not be bothered by having a homosexual neighbour, with Cabo Verde among four polled countries with a majority in favour. Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 of May 2020 placed Cabo Verde with Namibia and Sao Tome and Principe as particularly tolerant, while finding tolerance toward sexual minorities remarkably weak across the continent even among younger respondents.

Accounts describe Cabo Verde as among the most tolerant countries towards gay and lesbian people, occasionally described as the most tolerant regarding LGBT people. Subnational variation is reported. Sao Vicente is cited as relaxed and welcoming, which illustrates local difference within that national pattern rather than a separate legal regime.

Public LGBT organising has grown. No lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender organisations were recorded as active in the 2010 United States report. Associacao Gay de Cabo Verde had been established by 2013. The first pride parade was held in Mindelo in June 2013, with the first Praia pride three years later. The 2018 Pride Week in Praia combined a parade with campaigns by Associacao Gay de Cabo Verde, Associacao LGBTI de Praia and Associacao Arco Iris petitioning the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law.

Transgender people in Cabo Verde are often referred to locally as tchindas. Decriminalisation in 2004 made Cabo Verde the second country to decriminalise after South Africa.
localsOnly:
Residents seek workplace redress under the Labour Code provisions that apply to sexual orientation. Article 406(3) provides that a fine varying case by case applies also to unlawful dismissal based on racial grounds, belonging to a particular ethnic group, religious motives, sexual orientation or any other discriminatory reason.

The age of consent was 16 for consensual homosexual and heterosexual acts at decriminalisation. It was reported as 14 as of 2015.

For residents, no procedure for change of legal name to reflect gender or change of gender marker is sourced beyond the 2016 refusal in the Andrade case.
outOfScopeNotes:
Not sourced as law or procedure: rules on change of gender markers on documents, screening that could risk outing, segregated facilities, custody, or medical care for transgender people. The inventory records no statute, provision, penalty or procedure on these points.

Unresolved on social attitudes: no documented statement about societal tolerance specifically toward transgender people was sourced. All tolerance findings are framed around gay, lesbian, homosexual neighbours or LGBT people generally.

Not sourced beyond 2016: any later statute or administrative procedure creating legal gender recognition.
